prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

(CNN) -- A Colorado prosecutor Friday asked a judge to dismiss the first-degree murder charge against Tim Masters, who spent nine years in prison until new DNA evidence indicated someone else might have committed the crime. Tim Masters, center, walks out of a Fort Collins, Colorado, courthouse Tuesday with his attorney David Wymore. Court papers filed by District Attorney Larry Abrahamson cited "newly discovered" evidence, but took pains to state that evidence didn't clear Masters. "While the newly discovered DNA evidence does not exonerate Timothy Masters, it clearly warrants a complete re-examination of all the evidence related to the murder of Peggy Hettrick," the court papers state. The motion seeks dismissal of the charges "in the interest of justice." It points out the DNA testing used to uncover the new evidence wasn't available when Masters was investigated and tried. On Tuesday a judge threw out Masters' 1999 murder conviction, and he was freed -- also "in the interest of justice." Although the motion signals that Abrahamson is dropping the Masters case, he did not rule out future prosecution. In a statement, the prosecutor cautioned: "Contrary to news reports, the DNA testing results only suggest that there may be others, along with Timothy Masters, who should be investigated. These test results do not provide us with enough information to completely exonerate anyone." Abrahamson said he has asked Colorado Attorney General John Suthers to appoint a special prosecutor to continue the investigation of Hettrick's slaying. The attorney general will announce his decision early next week, Abrahamson said. Masters, 36, has been investigated for Hettrick's  murder since he was 15. He has insisted he had nothing to do with her death, and no physical evidence ties him directly to the crime.  Watch Masters describe his anger at police » . A jury convicted Masters 12 years after the discovery of Hettrick's stabbed and sexually mutilated corpse in a field near his trailer. Among the evidence jurors considered were a collection of knives found in Master's bedroom, gruesome sketches and testimony from a prosecution expert that he fit the psychological profile of a killer. Masters' defense team said he was framed, and that police and prosecutors sat on evidence that could have raised doubt about his guilt. The significance of Friday's motion to dismiss is largely procedural, but Abrahamson indicated earlier this week that it might be unnecessary to try Masters again. "In light of newly discovered evidence revealed to me on Friday," Abrahamson said in a statement a week ago, "I will be moving as expeditiously as possible to make the determination of whether all charges against Timothy Masters will be dismissed." Abrahamson also has vowed to review all "contested convictions" in which advances in DNA testing may prove useful. He said he wanted to examine the legal discovery process and that he had met with the Fort Collins police chief and his officers "to discuss the critical flow of information with assurance that all information is available to our office and the defense." Special prosecutor Don Quick filed a motion earlier this month citing four instances in which police and prosecutors should have handed over evidence to Masters' original defense team.  See the key players in the case » . Among them was a police interview with a plastic surgeon who said it was improbable that a teen could have made the meticulous cuts necessary to remove Hettrick's body parts. Also, according to Quick's motion, police failed to divulge that a renowned FBI profiler warned police that Masters' penchant for doodling gruesome horror scenes did not tie him to the crime. Investigations into how police and prosecutors handled the case continue. E-mail to a friend .

outputs.L2:
(CNN) — On Friday, a Colorado prosecutor requested that a judge drop the first-degree murder charge against Tim Masters, who served nine years in prison before newly obtained DNA findings suggested another person may have been involved in the killing.

Masters, accompanied by attorney David Wymore, left a Fort Collins, Colorado, courthouse on Tuesday.

In documents submitted to the court, District Attorney Larry Abrahamson referred to the DNA results as newly uncovered evidence while emphasizing that they did not prove Masters’ innocence. The filing said that although the DNA findings did not exonerate Masters, they justified a comprehensive review of every piece of evidence connected to Peggy Hettrick’s murder.

The motion asked for the charge to be dismissed in the interests of justice. It also noted that the DNA technology that produced the new information did not exist when authorities investigated Masters and brought him to trial.

On Tuesday, a judge overturned Masters’ 1999 murder conviction and ordered his release, likewise citing the interests of justice.

Although Abrahamson’s motion indicated that he was ending the current case against Masters, the prosecutor left open the possibility that charges could be brought again. He warned in a statement that, despite media accounts, the test results merely indicated that other people might need to be investigated in addition to Masters. According to Abrahamson, the findings were insufficient to fully clear anyone.

Abrahamson said he had requested that Colorado Attorney General John Suthers designate a special prosecutor to continue investigating Hettrick’s killing. He added that the attorney general expected to announce a decision early the following week.

Masters, 36, had been under scrutiny in connection with Hettrick’s death since he was 15. He consistently denied any involvement, and no physical evidence directly connected him to the crime.

Hettrick’s stabbed and sexually mutilated body was found in a field close to Masters’ trailer. Twelve years later, a jury found him guilty. Evidence presented to jurors included several knives discovered in his bedroom, disturbing drawings, and testimony from a prosecution witness who said Masters matched the psychological characteristics of a murderer.

Masters’ attorneys maintained that he had been set up. They also alleged that police and prosecutors withheld material that could have created reasonable doubt about his guilt.

Friday’s dismissal request was mainly a procedural step. However, Abrahamson had suggested earlier in the week that a second trial might not be needed. In a statement issued one week earlier, he said that evidence newly disclosed to him the previous Friday would prompt him to decide as quickly as possible whether every charge against Masters should be dropped.

Abrahamson also promised to reassess all disputed convictions in which improvements in DNA analysis might be relevant. He said he intended to review procedures for sharing evidence in criminal cases. He also reported meeting with the Fort Collins police chief and other officers to address the essential exchange of information and ensure that all material reached both prosecutors and defense lawyers.

Earlier that month, special prosecutor Don Quick filed a motion identifying four occasions on which police and prosecutors should have provided evidence to Masters’ original legal team.

One example involved a police interview with a plastic surgeon. The doctor said it was unlikely that a teenager could have performed the precise cuts required to remove parts of Hettrick’s body. Quick’s filing also stated that police did not disclose a warning from a prominent FBI profiler, who said Masters’ habit of drawing graphic horror images did not connect him to the murder.

Investigations remained underway into the conduct of police and prosecutors in the case.

The results indicated that biological evidence found on Hettrick’s clothing came from people other than Masters, suggesting that others may have been involved and prompting authorities to undertake a complete re-examination of the case.

Hettrick was found murdered in Fort Collins in 1987, when Masters was 15 years old. Investigators focused on him early in the inquiry, although no physical evidence directly connected him to the crime. He was eventually convicted on circumstantial evidence and sentenced to life in prison.

Masters’s attorneys continued to challenge the conviction, arguing that important evidence had not been properly disclosed or considered. Advances in DNA technology later allowed evidence from the case to be tested more thoroughly. After reviewing the new findings and other questions surrounding the original investigation and prosecution, the district attorney concluded that the conviction could no longer stand as it was.

Masters was released after spending nine years in prison. The prosecutor also requested that a special prosecutor be appointed to conduct an independent review, including an examination of how the case was originally handled and whether another person could be responsible for Hettrick’s death.

Authorities stressed, however, that dismissing the charge did not amount to a formal declaration of innocence. They said the DNA evidence undermined the prosecution’s case but did not conclusively establish who killed Hettrick or fully eliminate Masters as a possible suspect. The charge was therefore dismissed in a way that left open the possibility of a future prosecution if additional evidence emerged.

The murder investigation remains open. Officials said they would continue reviewing the physical evidence, the conduct of the earlier investigation and any leads pointing to other suspects, while Masters’s attorneys maintained that his release was long overdue.
